assumption: Fidelity: any text of at most 255 characters is recorded as the choice and counted under its own name, as the original does; the ballot itself only ever sends a or b.
statement: Nothing checks that the choice is a or b: any text is recorded and counted under its own name in the standing, but left out of the shares and the total.

assumption: Fidelity: after a vote the ballot marks the chosen option, as the original does in normal operation over http; the script fetched from a public CDN is incarnation and not kept.
statement: The tick marking the voter's choice is drawn by jQuery fetched over plain http from a public CDN; a page served over https, or with the CDN unreachable, shows no confirmation although the vote was taken.

assumption: Left free: health checks and start order are incarnation; what the estate does while a part is unavailable is decided by the Fail visibly cases.
statement: The compose files check the ballot, the line of ballots and the tally for health and start each part only when what it needs is healthy; the swarm and Kubernetes manifests declare no health checks and no start order.

assumption: Fail visibly: once the record of votes is back after being unreachable, recording resumes without a restart and nothing taken in the meantime is lost.
statement: The idle keep-alive query is bound to the first tally connection; after a reconnect it still runs on the old one, which would fail and stop the recorder.

assumption: Fail visibly: a vote shown as taken outlives the replacement of any part in every deployment, Kubernetes included; the README's promise of a kept tally holds everywhere.
statement: Under Kubernetes the tally of votes and the line of ballots live in emptyDir scratch space, lost whenever their pod is replaced; the README says the tally is backed by a volume, which holds only for the swarm.

assumption: Fail visibly: a vote shown as taken but not yet counted outlives a restart of any part and is counted once the parts are back.
statement: In the swarm the line of ballots has no volume, so ballots taken but not yet counted are lost if it restarts.

assumption: Fidelity: a rebuild is not a redesign and adds no monitoring, alerting or backup capability; that acknowledged votes outlive a restart is decided under votes-outlive-a-restart.
statement: Nothing in production watches the estate's health, raises an alert, or backs up the votes: there is no monitoring, availability or backup capability to record.

assumption: Options are configuration kept for the life of a deployment: a is Cats and b is Dogs unless the operator says otherwise.
statement: No action creates, changes or ends an option: the operator names the two when deploying the ballot (OPTION_A and OPTION_B, defaulting to Cats and Dogs), and they last as long as that deployment. Neither the swarm nor the Kubernetes manifests set them, so production runs with the defaults.

assumption: Fix defects: a vote whose choice or voter identifier is longer than 255 characters is refused with the bad-request refusal and records nothing, and votes cast after it are still recorded. The ballot never sends such a value, so no one outside relies on it being answered with the page.
statement: A choice or voter identifier longer than 255 characters cannot be recorded: the insert and the replacement both fail, the vote is lost, and the part that records votes stops and must be restarted before later votes are counted.

assumption: The code wins: a voter's latest choice replaces the earlier one.
statement: The README says only one vote per browser is accepted and later votes are not registered; the code records the later vote in place of the earlier one, and the ballot itself says 'you can change your vote'.

assumption: Fail visibly: while ballots cannot be taken in, a vote is refused and the voter told so, or taken and kept; the original's timeouts and retries are its failure behaviour and are not kept, so no time bound is set.
statement: The ballot sets a 5 second socket timeout but the redis client version is not pinned; whether it also bounds connecting, and whether the client retries before failing, depends on the version installed.

assumption: Left free: how the results service is run, and its inspector, is incarnation nobody outside relies on.
statement: The development setup runs the results service under nodemon with the Node inspector open on port 9229; production runs node server.js under tini.

assumption: Fail visibly: the results service never gives up; while the record of votes is unreachable watchers are told so, and the standing is published again as soon as it is reachable.
statement: If the tally cannot be reached for 1000 attempts a second apart at start, the results service logs 'Giving up' and never publishes a standing again until restarted, while still serving a page that stays blank of numbers.

assumption: Fidelity: the results page names a Cats and b Dogs whatever the ballot calls them, as the original does; no production manifest sets OPTION_A or OPTION_B, so in normal operation the two pages agree.
statement: The ballot labels the options from OPTION_A and OPTION_B, but the results page always says Cats and Dogs, so a poll deployed with other labels reports under the wrong names.

assumption: Fail visibly: while the record of votes is unreachable no wrong standing is sent and watchers are told the standing cannot be counted; publishing resumes on its own once the record is back, without a restart.
statement: When the tally becomes unreachable after the results service has connected, the pg client's held connection may report the error to the pending count (logged, retried a second later) or raise an unhandled error that stops the service.

assumption: GET / answers with the results page.
statement: The GET / handler calls path.resolve, but path is never required, so it would fail with a 500; it is predicted never to run because the static handler registered first answers / with views/index.html.

assumption: Left free: the seed is a development tool, not part of the estate; no action seeds votes.
statement: The seed profile casts 3000 votes (2000 for a, 1000 for b, each as a new voter) against the ballot; it exists only in the development compose file.

assumption: Left free: the version of the store under the tally is incarnation.
statement: The results test stack runs the tally on postgres 9.4 while every other setup runs postgres 15.

assumption: Fix defects: of two votes by one voter, the one cast last is the one kept, whatever order the estate records them in.
statement: The swarm runs two recorders taking ballots off one line; two quick votes by the same voter can be recorded out of order, so the earlier choice can end up as the one counted.

assumption: Left free: the results page reads only a and b, so the order of other choices in the counts is not relied on; no case compares more than one of them.
statement: A choice other than a or b is added to the counts after a and b in the order the count query returns rows, which the query does not fix.

assumption: Left free: which server runs the ballot, and its debugger, is incarnation nobody outside relies on.
statement: The development setup runs the ballot from the dev stage with Flask's debug server and code reloading; production runs the final stage under gunicorn with four workers.

assumption: Fail visibly: a vote taken while the record of votes is unreachable is either refused to the voter or kept and recorded once the record is back; it is never dropped.
statement: A vote taken off the line while the tally's connection is not open is dropped: the recorder reconnects instead of recording it.

assumption: Left free: nobody relies on the form or length of a new identifier; it need only be non-empty and distinct from every identifier already handed out.
statement: The new voter identifier drops the last hexadecimal digit (a Python 2 habit of trimming a trailing L), so it carries 60 random bits and is shorter when it starts with zeros. Intended or not, identifiers can collide sooner.
